newsitem.title: GERMANY: VW early retirement plan no panacea - employers.
newsitem.headline: VW early retirement plan no panacea - employers.

text.p: German employers on Wednesday said the early retirement scheme agreed by car-maker Volkswagen AG for its 90,000 workers late on Tuesday was not necessarily a solution for other firms in the sector.

Under the VW scheme -- which will cost an estimated 150,000 marks for each participant -- workers aged 55 may opt to take 85 percent of their net income for the next five years and in return can retire at 57-1/2 years instead of 60.
VW will also make top-up pension payments to make sure that workers do not see any significant cut to the level of their pension upon retirement.
"Without having thoroughly analysed the deal, I can say that it is probably -- probably -- a touch too expensive for us," said Anton Hunger, spokesman for luxury sports-car maker Porsche AG.
"Big companies negotiate different arrangements to the smaller ones -- and we clearly rank among the smaller ones compared to Volkswagen," he added.

Resistance by employers to the scheme, which Volkswagen says will enable it to pare down its workforce while still taking on new trainees, was made clear by the collapse of regional employer-union talks on Wednesday that had aimed at introducing such arrangements in sector-wide wage contracts.

Speaking just before the talks in the large southern state of Baden-Wuerttemberg broke down, an official for the Gesamtmetall employers federation there said it could not support a scheme such as the VW pact.

"We cannot agree to sector-wide contracts that would impose such additional costs on our members," Peer-Michael Dick, business manager for the Baden-Wuerttemberg metal and engineering employers federation told German radio.
He added that the VW retirement deal must not be taken in isolation and was in fact accompanied by other agreements, including on shift-work arrangements, that were favourable to Volkswagen.

Talks between employers and unions in Baden-Wuerttemberg, home to Daimler-Benz AG's main Mercedes factory, eventually stalled because employers insisted that firms should have the final say as to whether they offer such a scheme.

But IG Metall, the huge metal and engineering trade union that sees early retirement as a way to reduce Germany's record jobless toll, indicated on Wednesday that it may seek to have its way yet by organising industrial action on the issue.

"If it comes to it, we shall not shy away from industrial action," Gerhard Zambelli, regional head of the IG Metall metal and engineering sector trade union, told reporters after the collapse of the talks.

Whether it can mobilise worker support as it did last year when firms such as Daimler were forced to back down on planned cuts to sick pay entitlements is unclear -- thus far, worker protests have involved thousands rather than the hundreds of thousands who took to the streets last November.

But if it does, firms such as Porsche, which unlike the mighty Volkswagen is not able to conclude its own "house agreements" but is bound by regional pacts, will find themselves having to offer early retirement anyway.
